content.thinking:
I need to be careful to use the named figures rather than writing out any numbers myself. I'm noting the key facts for alert AL1 — the comparison between A1 and A2, the widest gap in A3, the single purchase in A4, the oldest purchase timing in A5, and when caching resumed in A6 — and thinking through how to express the span between when the cache stopped keeping up and when service resumed.

The root cause is bounded by what the record actually shows: the cache diverged from the ledger starting at A5, with confirmed evidence like the discarded entries in M1, but nothing explains the mechanism behind why it stopped updating. I'm tracing the causal chain from stale totals back through the cache falling behind, while noting the absence of any logged changes, flag changes, or readable metrics that could explain the stoppage, plus considering the detection delay as a contributing factor.

I'm drafting action items: continuous reconciliation checks with earlier alerting, restoring readable logs/metrics for the cache-update path, and a dedicated investigation into why the cache stopped syncing at A5. I'm framing the executive summary to avoid unsupported numbers, sticking to named durations and confirmed facts only.

I'm also listing assumptions and open gaps — duration is a lower bound, root cause unestablished, the PR unreviewed, error rate unknown — while noting what went well (fast mitigation, confirmed cleanup), what went wrong (empty investigator metrics/logs, stale entries served before detection), and what went right by luck (minimal purchase impact since the ledger stayed accurate as a fallback).

action_items.item: Run the cache-versus-ledger reconciliation check continuously, and alert on the lag between the newest purchase and the newest cached update, so drift is caught soon after it starts and not after stale figures are already served.
Make io-shop per-minute metrics and logs readable and retained for the cache-update path, so an investigation can see what the cache was doing when it stopped keeping up.
Find out why io-summary-cache stopped applying purchases from {A5}, using the cache's update path and the ledger feed, and record the answer in this postmortem.
Add an automatic repair for drifting cache entries, such as invalidating an entry when the ledger has a newer purchase, so recovery does not depend on someone discarding the cache by hand.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers were shown cached spend totals that were behind their real purchases: {A1} of {A2} figures disagreed with the ledger, the widest gap being {A3} and the most any one figure was missing being {A4} purchase. No requests failed; only the reconciliation check showed it.
The copies being served from {A6} lacked purchases recorded after {A5}, while the purchase ledger itself was correct, so the cached copies were the only thing wrong.

The spend-totals cache stopped keeping up with the ledger from {A5}, and nothing was putting the copies right, so a total went stale as soon as its shopper bought again. Discarding the {A1} stale entries removed everything that was wrong and sent pages back to the ledger.

Why the cache stopped updating is not answered by the record: no production changes, no flag changes and no log lines were found around the onset, and the per-minute metrics could not be read. The chain stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: Nothing reconciles the cache against the ledger or repairs a drifting copy, so stale entries persist and grow as shoppers buy again. The mitigation only discards entries and does not fix the update path.

Detection came only from the alert's reconciliation check. Copies stopped keeping up at {A5} and were being served from {A6}, and the alert was raised at {alert_raised}. Request metrics stay flat for this kind of fault.
The investigation could not see the incident: zero minutes of metrics and zero log lines were read for the service, so the cause of the cache stopping could not be established.

input.executive_summary: Some shoppers on io-shop were shown spend totals that were out of date. {A1} of {A2} cached totals disagreed with the purchases behind them. The purchase records were correct throughout, and the most any one total was missing was {A4} purchase, a gap of at most {A3}. The copies stopped keeping up from {A5} and were being served from {A6}. The service was affected for at least {duration}, a lower bound because the service had not recovered when metrics were last read. Argus was alerted at {alert_raised} and discarded the stale copies, so pages go back to the correct purchase records. The store confirmed it removed what was wrong. Nothing has yet been shown to be keeping the copies correct, and the reason they stopped updating is unknown. A draft fix is awaiting review.

got_lucky: The purchase ledger stayed correct, so discarding the copies sent pages back to a reliable source.
The drift was small: at most {A4} purchase was missing from any one figure, a gap of at most {A3}.
went_well: The alert's reconciliation check found drift that no service metric showed.
Argus acted quickly on the leading candidate. The discard was confirmed, and the store reported removing everything that was wrong.
A draft fix was proposed for review soon after mitigation.
went_wrong: Metrics and logs for the incident could not be read, so the cause of the cache stopping was never established and the error rate is unknown.
Stale figures were served from {A6} before the alert at {alert_raised}.
The mitigation clears the current stale entries but does not stop the cache from drifting again.

input.root_cause: The cache of shopper spend totals (io-summary-cache) stopped keeping up with the purchase ledger from {A5} and nothing in the system detected or repaired the drift, so out-of-date totals were served. The record does not show why the cache stopped updating: no change, flag change or log line explains it.
